arXiv:2007.16003v2 [math.AP] 05 Jan 2021

Blow-up and lifespan estimate for generalized Tricomi equations related to Glassey conjecture

Ning-An Lai Note:  Institute of Nonlinear Analysis and Department of Mathematics, Lishui University, No. 1 Xueyuan Rd., Lishui City 323000, Zhejiang, China. E-mail: ninganlai@lsu.edu.cn    Nico Michele Schiavone Note:  Department of Mathematics, Sapienza University of Rome, P.le Aldo Moro 5, Roma 00185, Italy. E-mail: schiavone@mat.uniroma1.it
Keywords:generalized Tricomi equations, semilinear, derivative nonlinearity, blow-up, lifespanMSC2020:primary 35L71, secondary 35B44 \begin{array}[]{ll}\mbox{\footnotesize{\bf Keywords:}}&\mbox{\footnotesize generalized Tricomi equations, semilinear, derivative nonlinearity, blow-up, lifespan}\\ \mbox{\footnotesize{\bf MSC2020:}}&\mbox{\footnotesize primary 35L71, secondary 35B44 }\\ \end{array}
Abstract

We study in this paper the small data Cauchy problem for the semilinear generalized Tricomi equations with a nonlinear term of derivative type

ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|pu_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}

for m≥0m\geq 0. Blow-up result and lifespan estimate from above are established for 1<p≤1+2(m+1)​(n−1)−m1<p\leq 1+\frac{2}{(m+1)(n-1)-m}. If m=0m=0, our results coincide with those of the semilinear wave equation. The novelty consists in the construction of a new test function, by combining cut-off functions, the modified Bessel function and a harmonic function. Interestingly, if n=2n=2 the blow-up power is independent of mm. We also furnish a local existence result, which implies the optimality of lifespan estimate at least in the 11-dimensional case.

1 Introduction

In this work, we consider the small data Cauchy problem for the semilinear generalized Tricomi equations with a power-nonlinearity of derivative type

{ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|pin [0,T)×ℝn,u(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x)x∈ℝn,\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}\quad\text{in $[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$},\\ &u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\quad u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x)\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

where m≥0m\geq 0 is a real constant, n≥1n\geq 1 is the dimension and ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 is a “small” parameter. The initial data f,gf,g are compactly supported functions from the energy spaces

f∈H1​(ℝn),g∈H1−1m+1​(ℝn),f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\quad g\in H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),

and, without loss of generality, we may assume

supp(f,g)⊂{x∈ℝn:|x|≤1}.\displaystyle\supp(f,g)\subset\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|x|\leq 1\}. (1.2)

Recently, the semilinear generalized Tricomi equations attract more and more attention, due to their physical background. In dimension n=1n=1 and for m=1/2m=1/2, the equation

ut​t−t​ux​x=0u_{tt}-tu_{xx}=0

is the classical linear Tricomi equation, which was introduced by Tricomi [44] in the context of boundary value problems for partial differential equations of mixed type. The Tricomi equation appears in gas dynamic problems, connected to gas flows with nearly sonic speed, describing the transition from subsonic flow (t<0t<0) to supersonic flow (t>0t>0), see Frankl [10]. We refer to Yagdjian [47, 48, 49, 50, 51] and references therein for more details.

For k>0k>0 and n≥1n\geq 1, the operator

𝒯=∂t2−tkΔ\mathcal{T}=\partial_{t}^{2}-t^{k}\Delta (1.3)

appearing in (1.1) is also known as Gellerstedt operator. The first direction in the study of (generalized) Tricomi equations is to construct the explicit fundamental solution. Barros-Neto and Gelfand [3, 4, 5] first established the fundamental solution for

y​ux​x+uy​y=0yu_{xx}+u_{yy}=0

in the whole plane. For the Gellerstedt operator (1.3) with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, Yagdjian [47] constructed a fundamental solution relative to an arbitrary point (t0,x0)∈[0,+∞)×ℝn(t_{0},x_{0})\in[0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^{n} with support located in the “forward cone” D⁡(t0,x0)={(t,x)∈ℝn+1:(k+2)​|x−x0|≤2​(t−t0)k/2+1}D(t_{0},x_{0})=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\colon(k+2)|x-x_{0}|\leq 2(t-t_{0})^{k/2+1}\}.

Recently, the long time behavior of solutions for small data Cauchy problem to the semilinear generalized Tricomi equation

{ut​t−tk​Δ​u=|u|p,in [0,T)×ℝnu(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x)x∈ℝn,\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{tt}-t^{k}\Delta u=|u|^{p},\quad\text{in $[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$}\\ &u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\quad u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x)\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\end{aligned}\right. (1.4)

comes into interest. The main goal is to determine the critical power pc​(k,n)p_{c}(k,n) such that, if 1<p≤pc​(k,n)1<p\leq p_{c}(k,n) then the solution blows up in a finite time, while if p>pc​(k,n)p>p_{c}(k,n) there is a unique global-in-time solution. Yagdjian [48] obtained some partial results, in the sense that there was still a gap between the blow-up and global existence ranges. The critical power is finally established in a recent series of works by He, Witt and Yin [14, 15, 16, 17] (see also the Doctoral dissertation by He [13]). For k≥1k\geq 1, pc​(k,n)p_{c}(k,n) admits the following form:

  • •

    if n=1n=1, then pc​(k,1)=1+4k\displaystyle p_{c}(k,1)=1+\frac{4}{k};

  • •

    if n≥2n\geq 2, then pc​(k,n)p_{c}(k,n) is the positive root of the quadratic equation

    2+[n+1−3​(1−2k+2)]​p−[n−1+(1−2k+2)]​p2=0.2+\left[n+1-3\left(1-\frac{2}{k+2}\right)\right]p-\left[n-1+\left(1-\frac{2}{k+2}\right)\right]p^{2}=0.

Recently, Lin and Tu [30] studied the upper bound of lifespan estimate for (1.4), and Ikeda, Lin and Tu [21] established the blow-up and upper bound of lifespan estimate for the weakly coupled system of the generalized Tricomi equations with multiple propagation speed. The critical power above should be compared with the corresponding one for the semilinear wave equation ut​t−Δ​u=|u|pu_{tt}-\Delta u=|u|^{p}. Indeed, letting k=0k=0 in the definition of pc​(k,n)p_{c}(k,n), we infer pc​(0,1)=+∞p_{c}(0,1)=+\infty and, for n≥2n\geq 2, pc​(0,n)p_{c}(0,n) becomes the so-called Strauss exponent, which is exactly the critical power for the small data Cauchy problem in (1.4) with k=0k=0 (see e.g. [26] and references therein for background and results about this problem). Finally, we refer also to Ruan, Witt and Yin [36, 37, 38, 39] for results about the local existence and local singularity structure of low regularity solutions for the equation ut​t−tk​Δ​u=f⁡(t,x,u)u_{tt}-t^{k}\Delta u=f(t,x,u).

In this paper, we consider the semilinear generalized Tricomi equations with power-nonlinearity of derivative type, focusing on blow-up result and lifespan estimate from above for the small data Cauchy problem. Note that, setting m=0m=0 in (1.1), we come back to the semilinear wave equation

ut​t−Δ​u=|ut|p.u_{tt}-\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}. (1.5)

For this problem, Glassey [11] conjectured that the critical exponent is the power, now named after him, defined by

pG(n):={1+2n−1if n≥2,+∞if n=1.p_{G}(n):=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1+\frac{2}{n-1}&\text{if $n\geq 2$,}\\ &+\infty&\text{if $n=1$.}\end{aligned}\right. (1.6)

The research on this problem was initiated by John [24], where more general equations in dimension n=3n=3 are considered, proving the blow-up of solutions for p=2p=2. Then, the study of the blow-up was continued in the low dimensional case by Masuda [32], Schaeffer [41], John [25] and Agemi [2], whereas Rammaha [33] treated the high dimensional case n≥4n\geq 4 under radial symmetric assumptions. Finally, Zhou [52] proved the blow-up for n≥1n\geq 1 and 1<p≤pG​(n)1<p\leq p_{G}(n), furnishing the upper bound for the lifespan of the solutions, namely

Tε≤{C​ε−2​(p−1)2−(n−1)​(p−1)if 1<p<pG​(n),exp⁡(C​ε−(p−1))if p=pG​(n),T_{\varepsilon}\leq\left\{\begin{aligned} &C{\varepsilon}^{-\frac{2(p-1)}{2-(n-1)(p-1)}}&&\text{if $1<p<p_{G}(n)$,}\\ &\exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-(p-1)})&&\text{if $p=p_{G}(n)$,}\end{aligned}\right. (1.7)

for some positive constant CC independent of ε{\varepsilon}. We recall that the lifespan TεT_{\varepsilon} is defined as the maximal existence time of the solution, depending on the parameter ε{\varepsilon}. Regarding the global existence part, we refer to Sideris [42], Hidano and Tsutaya [18] and Tzvetkov [45] for results in dimension n=2,3n=2,3 and Hidano, Wang and Yokoyama [19] for the high dimensional cases n≥4n\geq 4 under radially symmetric assumptions. For more details about the Glassey conjecture, one can read the references [28] and [46].

The study of problem (1.1) under consideration generalize the Glassey conjecture. Therefore, it is interesting to find the critical exponent and lifespan estimate for (1.1), which will coincide with the Glassey exponent (1.6) and Zhou’s lifespan estimate (1.7) respectively for m=0m=0. The main tool here used is the test function method. In [15], the blow-up result for (1.4) is based on a test function given by the product of the harmonic function ∫Sn−1ex⋅ω​𝑑ω\int_{S^{n-1}}e^{x\cdot\omega}d\omega and the solution of the ordinary differential equation

λ′′​(t)−tk​λ′​(t)=0.\lambda^{\prime\prime}(t)-t^{k}\lambda^{\prime}(t)=0.

Inspired by the works [22] and [29], we construct a nonnegative test function composed by a cut-off function, the harmonic function ∫Sn−1ex⋅ω​𝑑ω\int_{S^{n-1}}e^{x\cdot\omega}d\omega and the solution of the ODE (4.1) below. Since we consider the Tricomi-type equations with derivative nonlinear term, the first derivative with respect to time variable and a factor t−2​mt^{-2m} are included in the special test function. Before proving the blow-up result, we give also a local existence result following the approach of Yagdjian [48], from which we can deduce the optimality of the lifespan estimates at least for n=1n=1.

When this work was almost finished, we found the paper [31] by Lucente and Palmieri, where they independently studied the same problem with a different approach. However, the result we are going to present here improves the blow-up range and lifespan estimates they found.

We cite also the very recent papers [7] by Chen, Lucente and Palmieri and [12] by Hamouda and Hamza, where the blow-up phenomena for generalized Tricomi equations with combined linearity, i.e. ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|p+|u|qu_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}+|u|^{q}, is independently studied exploiting the iteration argument. In particular, the work [12] confirms the blow-up result presented in this paper by giving an alternative proof. Conversely, we are confident that also our method can be adapted to study various blow-up problems involving generalized Tricomi equations, including the combined nonlinearity. This means that the test function method presented in this work and the iteration argument developed in [7, 12] furnish two different approaches for the study of blow-up phenomena for Tricomi-related problems.

2 Main Result

Let us start stating the definition of energy solution for our problem (1.1), similarly as in [22] and [27].

Definition 1.

We say that the function

u∈C⁡([0,T),H1​(ℝn))∩C1​([0,T),H1−1m+1​(ℝn)),with ut∈Llocp​((0,T)×ℝn),u\in C([0,T),H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}))\cap C^{1}([0,T),H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n})),\quad\text{with $u_{t}\in L_{\rm loc}^{p}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n})$},

is a weak solution of (1.1) on [0,T)[0,T) if u⁡(0,x)=ε​f​(x)u(0,x)={\varepsilon}f(x) in H1​(ℝn)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), ut​(0,x)=ε​g​(x)u_{t}(0,x)={\varepsilon}g(x) in H1−1m+1​(ℝn)H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and

ε​∫ℝng⁡(x)​Ψ​(0,x)​𝑑x+∫0T∫ℝn|ut|p​Ψ​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t=∫0T∫ℝn−ut(t,x)Ψt(t,x)dxdt+∫0T∫ℝnt2​m∇u(t,x)⋅∇Ψ(t,x)dxdt,\begin{split}&{\varepsilon}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g(x)\Psi(0,x)dx+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|u_{t}|^{p}\Psi(t,x)\,dxdt\\ =&\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}-u_{t}(t,x)\Psi_{t}(t,x)\,dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}t^{2m}\nabla u(t,x)\cdot\nabla\Psi(t,x)\,dxdt,\end{split} (2.1)

for any Ψ⁡(t,x)∈C01​([0,T)×ℝn)∩C∞​((0,T)×ℝn)\Psi(t,x)\in C^{1}_{0}\left([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\right)\cap C^{\infty}\left((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\right).

Remark 1.

The choice of the functional spaces H1​(ℝn)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and H1−1m+1​(ℝn)H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) for the initial data u⁡(0,x)u(0,x) and ut​(0,x)u_{t}(0,x) respectively are suggested by [13] and by Theorem 2 below. Of course, if m=0m=0 we have H0​(ℝn)=L2​(ℝn)H^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{n})=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

In the same spirit of [26], let us define the exponent

pT(n,m):={1+2(m+1)​(n−1)−mif n≥2,+∞if n=1,p_{T}(n,m):=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1+\frac{2}{(m+1)(n-1)-m}&&\text{if $n\geq 2$,}\\ &+\infty&&\text{if $n=1$,}\end{aligned}\right.

as the root (when n≥2n\geq 2) of the expression γT​(n,m,p)=0\gamma_{T}(n,m;p)=0, where

γT​(n,m,p):=2−[(m+1)​(n−1)−m]​(p−1),\gamma_{T}(n,m;p):=2-[(m+1)(n-1)-m](p-1),

and observe that γT​(n,m,p)>0\gamma_{T}(n,m;p)>0 for 1<p<pT​(n,m)1<p<p_{T}(n,m).

We state now our main result for (1.1).

Theorem 1.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, m≥0m\geq 0 and 1<p≤pT​(n,m).1<p\leq p_{T}(n,m). Assume that f∈H1​(ℝn)f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), g∈H1−1m+1​(ℝn)g\in H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) satisfy the compact support assumption (1.2) and that

a⁡(m)​f+g,a⁡(m):=[2​(m+1)]mm+1​Γ​(12+m2​(m+1))​Γ​(12−m2​(m+1))−1,a(m)f+g,\quad a(m):=[2(m+1)]^{\frac{m}{m+1}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{m}{2(m+1)}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{m}{2(m+1)}\right)}^{-1}, (2.2)

is non-negative and not identically vanishing. Suppose that uu is an energy solution of (1.1) with compact support in the “cone”

suppu∈{(t,x)∈[0,T)×ℝn:|x|≤γ⁡(t):=1+tm+1m+1}.\supp u\in\left\{(t,x)\in[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\colon|x|\leq\gamma(t):=1+\frac{t^{m+1}}{m+1}\right\}. (2.3)

Then, there exists a constant ε0=ε0​(f,g,m,n,p)>0{\varepsilon}_{0}={\varepsilon}_{0}(f,g,m,n,p)>0 such that the lifespan TεT_{\varepsilon} has to satisfy

Tε≤{C​ε−2​(p−1)γT​(n,m,p)if 1<p<pT​(n,m),exp⁡(C​ε−(p−1))if p=pT​(n,m),T_{\varepsilon}\leq\left\{\begin{aligned} &C{\varepsilon}^{-\frac{2(p-1)}{\gamma_{T}(n,m;p)}}&&\text{if $1<p<p_{T}(n,m)$,}\\ &\exp\left(C{\varepsilon}^{-(p-1)}\right)&&\text{if $p=p_{T}(n,m)$,}\end{aligned}\right. (2.4)

for 0<ε≤ε00<{\varepsilon}\leq{\varepsilon}_{0} and some constant CC independent of ε{\varepsilon}.

Remark 2.

For m=0m=0 the exponent pTp_{T} becomes the Glassey exponent (1.6), namely pT​(n,0)=pG​(n)p_{T}(n,0)=p_{G}(n), and the lifespan estimate (2.4) is exactly the same as (1.7).

Remark 3.

It is interesting to see that, if n=2n=2, then the blow-up power pT​(2,m)=3p_{T}(2,m)=3 and the subcritical lifespan estimate Tε≤C​ε−(1p−1−12)−1T_{\varepsilon}\leq C{\varepsilon}^{-\left(\frac{1}{p-1}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}} are independent of mm, whereas the lifespan for the “critical” power p=pT​(n,m)p=p_{T}(n,m) is independent of mm for every dimension.

Remark 4.

We conjecture that pT​(n,m)p_{T}(n,m) is indeed the critical exponent for problem (1.1) and the lifespan (2.4) are optimal. The next goal is to verify this conjecture considering the global-in-time existence for solutions to (1.1).

3 Local existence result

Before to proceed with the demonstration of Theorem 1 in Section 4, we firstly want to present in this section a local existence result. As observed in [31], it is possible to prove a local-in-time existence result for problem (1.1), regardless the size of the Cauchy data, following the steps in Section 2.1 of [8]. However, we believe that the following Theorem 2 is interesting to justify the choice of the energy space for the solution and the initial data in Theorem 1. In addition, we can verify the optimality of the lifespan estimate in the 11-dimensional case.

Let us consider the integral equation

u⁡(t,x)=ε​V1​(t,Dx)​f​(x)+ε​V2​(t,Dx)​g​(x)+∫0t[V2(t,Dx)V1(s,Dx)−V1(t,Dx)V2(s,Dx)]|ut(s,x)|pds\begin{split}u(t,x)=&\,{\varepsilon}V_{1}(t,D_{x})f(x)+{\varepsilon}V_{2}(t,D_{x})g(x)\\ &+\int_{0}^{t}[V_{2}(t,D_{x})V_{1}(s,D_{x})-V_{1}(t,D_{x})V_{2}(s,D_{x})]|u_{t}(s,x)|^{p}ds\end{split} (3.1)

where ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 is not necessarily small, f∈H1​(ℝn)f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), g∈H1−1m+1​(ℝn)g\in H^{1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and the Fourier multiplier V1​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}) and V2​(t,Dx)V_{2}(t,D_{x}) are defined below. As remarked in [48], any classical or distributional solution to our problem (1.1) solves also the integral equation (3.1). We have the following result.

Theorem 2.

Let 0≤m<20\leq m<2, p>max⁡{2,1+n2}p>\max\left\{2,1+\frac{n}{2}\right\}, σ∈(n2−m2​(m+1),p−1−m2​(m+1))\sigma\in\left(\frac{n}{2}-\frac{m}{2(m+1)},p-1-\frac{m}{2(m+1)}\right) and f∈Hσ+1​(ℝn)f\in H^{\sigma+1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), g∈Hσ+1−1m+1​(ℝn)g\in H^{\sigma+1-\frac{1}{m+1}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). Then there exists a unique solution

u∈C⁡([0,T),H˙σ+m2​(m+1)+1​(ℝn))∩C1​([0,T),Hσ+m2​(m+1)​(ℝn))u\in C\left([0,T);\dot{H}^{\sigma+\frac{m}{2(m+1)}+1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\right)\cap C^{1}\left([0,T);{H}^{\sigma+\frac{m}{2(m+1)}}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\right)

to equation (3.1) for some T>0T>0.

Set z:=2​i​ϕ​(t)​|ξ|z:=2i\phi(t)|\xi|, ϕ⁡(t):=tm+1m+1\phi(t):=\frac{t^{m+1}}{m+1} and μ:=m2​(m+1)\mu:=\frac{m}{2(m+1)}. Then V1​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}) and V2​(t,Dx)V_{2}(t,D_{x}) are the Fourier multiplier

Remark 5.

In the case of the wave equation, i.e. when m=0m=0, the definitions of V1​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}) and V2​(t,Dx)V_{2}(t,D_{x}) should be understood taking the limit for m→0m\to 0 in their formulas. Indeed, using the identities 10.2.14, 13.6.3 and 13.6.14 in [1], we get

limm→0V1​(t,|ξ|)\displaystyle\lim_{m\to 0}V_{1}(t,|\xi|) =limμ→0Γ⁡(μ+12)​(z4)1/2−μ​Iμ−1/2​(z2)=cosh⁡(z2),\displaystyle=\lim_{\mu\to 0}\Gamma\left(\mu+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{z}{4}\right)^{1/2-\mu}I_{\mu-1/2}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)=\cosh\left(\frac{z}{2}\right),

where Iν​(w)I_{\nu}(w) is the modified Bessel function of first kind. Thus for m=0m=0 one recovers the well-known wave operators V1​(t,Dx)=cos⁡(t​−Δ)V_{1}(t,D_{x})=\cos(t\sqrt{-\Delta}) and V2​(t,Dx)=sin⁡(t​−Δ)−ΔV_{2}(t,D_{x})=\frac{\sin(t\sqrt{-\Delta})}{\sqrt{-\Delta}}.

As Yagdjian observes, there are two different phase functions of two different waves hidden in Φ⁡(a,c,z)\Phi(a,c;z). More precisely, for 0<arg⁡z<π0<\arg z<\pi, we can write (see also [23])

e−z/2Φ(a,c;z)=Γ⁡(c)Γ⁡(a)ez/2H+(a,c;z)+Γ⁡(c)Γ⁡(c−a)e−z/2H−(a,c;z)e^{-z/2}\Phi(a,c;z)=\frac{\Gamma(c)}{\Gamma(a)}e^{z/2}H_{+}(a,c;z)+\frac{\Gamma(c)}{\Gamma(c-a)}e^{-z/2}H_{-}(a,c;z) (3.6)

where

H+​(a,c,z)\displaystyle H_{+}(a,c;z) =e−i​π​(c−a)ei​π​(c−a)−e−i​π​(c−a)​1Γ⁡(c−a)​za−c​∫∞(0+)e−ω​ωc−a−1​(1−ωz)a−1​𝑑ω,\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-i\pi(c-a)}}{e^{i\pi(c-a)}-e^{-i\pi(c-a)}}\frac{1}{\Gamma(c-a)}z^{a-c}\int_{\infty}^{(0+)}e^{-\omega}\omega^{c-a-1}\left(1-\frac{\omega}{z}\right)^{a-1}d\omega,
H−​(a,c,z)\displaystyle H_{-}(a,c;z) =1ei​π​a−e−i​π​a​1Γ⁡(a)​z−a​∫∞(0+)e−ω​ωa−1​(1+ωz)c−a−1​𝑑ω.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{e^{i\pi a}-e^{-i\pi a}}\frac{1}{\Gamma(a)}z^{-a}\int_{\infty}^{(0+)}e^{-\omega}\omega^{a-1}\left(1+\frac{\omega}{z}\right)^{c-a-1}d\omega.

For |z|→∞|z|\to\infty and 0<arg⁡z<π0<\arg z<\pi, the following asymptotic estimates hold:

H+​(a,c,z)\displaystyle H_{+}(a,c;z) ∼za−c​[1+∑k=1∞(c−a)k​(1−a)kk!​z−k],\displaystyle\sim z^{a-c}\left[1+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(c-a)_{k}(1-a)_{k}}{k!}z^{-k}\right],
H−​(a,c,z)\displaystyle H_{-}(a,c;z) ∼(e−i​π​z)−a​[1+∑k=1∞(−1)k​(a)k​(1+a−c)kk!​z−k].\displaystyle\sim(e^{-i\pi}z)^{-a}\left[1+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}\frac{(a)_{k}(1+a-c)_{k}}{k!}z^{-k}\right].

Combining the asymptotic estimates for H+​(a,c,z)H_{+}(a,c;z) and H−​(a,c,z)H_{-}(a,c;z) with their definitions, one can infer, for 2​ϕ​(t)​|ξ|≥12\phi(t)|\xi|\geq 1, the relations

|∂tk∂ξβH+​(a,c,2​i​ϕ​(t)​|ξ|)|\displaystyle|\partial_{t}^{k}\partial_{\xi}^{\beta}H_{+}(a,c;2i\phi(t)|\xi|)| ≤Ca,c,m,k,β​(ϕ⁡(t)​|ξ|)a−c​⟨ξ⟩km+1−|β|,\displaystyle\leq C_{a,c,m,k,\beta}(\phi(t)|\xi|)^{a-c}\langle\xi\rangle^{\frac{k}{m+1}-|\beta|}, (3.7)
|∂tk∂ξβH−​(a,c,2​i​ϕ​(t)​|ξ|)|\displaystyle|\partial_{t}^{k}\partial_{\xi}^{\beta}H_{-}(a,c;2i\phi(t)|\xi|)| ≤Ca,c,m,k,β​(ϕ⁡(t)​|ξ|)−a​⟨ξ⟩km+1−|β|,\displaystyle\leq C_{a,c,m,k,\beta}(\phi(t)|\xi|)^{-a}\langle\xi\rangle^{\frac{k}{m+1}-|\beta|}, (3.8)

where ⟨ξ⟩=(1+|ξ|2)1/2\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^{2})^{1/2} are the Japanese brackets.

Finally, let us introduce for simplicity of notation the operators

W1​(s,t,Dx):=\displaystyle W_{1}(s,t,D_{x}):= V1​(t,Dx)​V2​(s,Dx),\displaystyle\,V_{1}(t,D_{x})V_{2}(s,D_{x}),
W2​(s,t,Dx):=\displaystyle W_{2}(s,t,D_{x}):= V2​(t,Dx)​V1​(s,Dx),\displaystyle\,V_{2}(t,D_{x})V_{1}(s,D_{x}),

whose symbols, if we set z:=2​i​ϕ​(t)​|ξ|z:=2i\phi(t)|\xi| and ζ:=2​i​ϕ​(s)​|ξ|\zeta:=2i\phi(s)|\xi|, are given by

W1​(s,t,|ξ|)\displaystyle W_{1}(s,t,|\xi|) =se−(z+ζ)/2Φ(μ,2μ;z)Φ(1−μ,2(1−μ);ζ),\displaystyle=se^{-(z+\zeta)/2}\Phi(\mu,2\mu;z)\Phi(1-\mu,2(1-\mu);\zeta),
W2​(s,t,|ξ|)\displaystyle W_{2}(s,t,|\xi|) =te−(z+ζ)/2Φ(μ,2μ;ζ)Φ(1−μ,2(1−μ);z).\displaystyle=te^{-(z+\zeta)/2}\Phi(\mu,2\mu;\zeta)\Phi(1-\mu,2(1-\mu);z).

The key estimates employed in the proof of Theorem 2 are given in Corollary 1, which comes straightforwardly from Theorem 3, and in Lemma 1. The estimates in the following Theorem 3, which are of independent interest, are obtained adapting the argument exploited by Yagdjian [48] and Reissig [34] for the case of the operators V1​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}) and V2​(t,Dx)V_{2}(t,D_{x}). In order to not weigh down the exposition, we postpone the proof of this theorem in Appendix C.

Theorem 3.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, m≥0m\geq 0, μ:=m2​(m+1)\mu:=\frac{m}{2(m+1)} and ψ∈C0∞​(ℝn)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). Then the following Lq−Lq′L^{q}-L^{q^{\prime}} estimates on the conjugate line, i.e. for 1q+1q′=1\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}=1, hold for 0<s≤t0<s\leq t and for all admissible q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2]:

  1. (i)

    if n⁡(1q−1q′)−1≤σ≤−μ+n⁡(1q−1q′)n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right)-1\leq\sigma\leq-\mu+n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right), then

    ‖(−Δ)−σW1(s,t,Dx)ψ‖Lq′≲(t/s)−m/2s1+[σ−n⁡(1q−1q′)]​(m+1)‖ψ‖Lq;\left\lVert(\sqrt{-\Delta})^{-\sigma}W_{1}(s,t,D_{x})\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q^{\prime}}}\\ \lesssim(t/s)^{-m/2}s^{1+\left[\sigma-n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right)\right](m+1)}\left\lVert\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q}};
  2. (ii)

    if n⁡(1q−1q′)−1≤σ≤−1+μ+n⁡(1q−1q′)n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right)-1\leq\sigma\leq-1+\mu+n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right), then

    ‖(−Δ)−σW2(s,t,Dx)ψ‖Lq′≲(t/s)−m/2s1+[σ−n⁡(1q−1q′)]​(m+1)‖ψ‖Lq;\left\lVert(\sqrt{-\Delta})^{-\sigma}W_{2}(s,t,D_{x})\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q^{\prime}}}\\ \lesssim(t/s)^{-m/2}s^{1+\left[\sigma-n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right)\right](m+1)}\left\lVert\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q}};
  3. (iii)

    if n⁡(1q−1q′)≤σ≤1−μ+n⁡(1q−1q′)n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right)\leq\sigma\leq 1-\mu+n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right), then

    if σ=n⁡(1q−1q′)\sigma=n\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}\right), then

    ‖(−Δ)−σ​∂tW2​(s,t,Dx)​ψ‖Lq′≲(t/s)m/2​‖ψ‖Lq.\left\lVert(\sqrt{-\Delta})^{-\sigma}\partial_{t}W_{2}(s,t,D_{x})\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q^{\prime}}}\\ \lesssim(t/s)^{m/2}\left\lVert\psi\right\rVert_{L^{q}}.
Remark 6.

As in Yagdjian [48], it is easy to obtain similar estimates for the (homogeneous) Besov spaces and then for the Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces.

In the previous theorem, choosing q=q′=2q=q^{\prime}=2, σ=−1\sigma=-1 for W1​(s,t,Dx)W_{1}(s,t,D_{x}) and W2​(s,t,Dx)W_{2}(s,t,D_{x}) and σ=0\sigma=0 in the case of their derivatives, we immediately get the following corollary.

The following estimates hold

‖Wj​(s,t,Dx)​ψ‖H˙γ+1\displaystyle\left\lVert W_{j}(s,t,D_{x})\psi\right\rVert_{\dot{H}^{\gamma+1}} ≲(ts)−m/2‖ψ‖H˙γ,\displaystyle\lesssim(ts)^{-m/2}\left\lVert\psi\right\rVert_{\dot{H}^{\gamma}},

for n≥1n\geq 1, m≥0m\geq 0, γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R} and j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}.

Now we furnish estimates in the energy space H˙γ​(ℝn)\dot{H}^{\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and Hγ​(ℝn){H}^{\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) also for V1​(t,Dx),V2​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}),V_{2}(t,D_{x}) and their derivatives respect to time.

Let γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}, m≥0m\geq 0 and μ:=m2​(m+1)\mu:=\frac{m}{2(m+1)}. The following estimates hold:

    When ν∈ℤ\nu\in\mathbb{Z}, the right hand-side of this equation is replaced by its limiting value.

    where Γ\Gamma is the Gamma function.

Appendix C Proof of Theorem 3

In this appendix we prove the Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimates on the conjugate line for W1​(s,t,Dx)W_{1}(s,t,D_{x}), W2​(s,t,Dx)W_{2}(s,t,D_{x}) and their derivatives respect to time collected in Theorem 3. The argument is adapted from the proof of Theorem 3.3 by Yagdjian [48] (see also [34] and [9, Chapter 16]), where similar estimates for V1​(t,Dx)V_{1}(t,D_{x}) and V2​(t,Dx)V_{2}(t,D_{x}) are presented. Note that in [48] the additional hypothesis σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 is supposed, but this can be dropped, as we will show.

Before to proceed, we recall the following key lemmata.
